From Wiktionary, the free dictionary
See also: selfié and Selfie

English

[edit]

Etymology

[edit]

From self +‎ -ie. Attested since 2002, originally Australian English.

Pronunciation

[edit]
  • (General American, Received Pronunciation) IPA(key): /ˈsɛlfi/
  • Audio (UK):(file)
  • Rhymes: -ɛlfi

Noun

[edit]

selfie (plural selfies)

  2. (informal, mobile telephony, social media) A photographic self-portrait, especially one taken manually (not using a timer, tripod etc.) with a small camera or mobile phone.
    take a selfie
    • 2002 September 13, N. "Hopey" Hope, “re: Dissolvable stitches”, in ABC Online Forum‎[1], archived from the original on 23 November 2013:
      Um, drunk at a mates[sic] 21st, I tripped ofer[sic] and landed lip first (with front teeth coming a very close second) on a set of steps. I had a hole about 1cm long right through my bottom lip. And sorry about the focus, it was a selfie.
    • 2004 October 21, Brian McGuirk, “bmcguirk's photos.”, in Flickr‎[2], archived from the original on 26 November 2004:
      Pre. Nice rooftop selfie. […] No Hair. Another nice rooftop selfie.
    • 2005, Jim Krause, Photo Idea Index, HOW Books, published 2005, →ISBN, page 148:
      That's not to imply that it's "wrong" for your arm or hand to show up in a selfie.
    • 2012 December 27, Andrew Prince, “The Mars Rover Takes A Selfie”, in National Public Radio‎[3], archived from the original on 14 September 2015:
      The Mars Rover Takes A Selfie [title]
    • 2013 December 13, Brooke Gladstone, quoting Roberto Schmidt, “The Photographer Behind ‘Selfie-Gate’”, On the Media”, in National Public Radio‎[4], archived from the original on 1 January 2026:
      Barack Obama was talking to David Cameron and with the Danish Prime Minister, and that’s when she actually reached into her purse and brought out a cell phone and stretched her arms and did a selfie with them.
    • 2017 August 8, “Say Cheese”, in Lily's Driftwood Bay, season 2, episode 2, spoken by Lord Stag (Stephen Fry):
      I shall take this photograph myself. This must be what they call a selfie.
    • 2018, “She Works Out Too Much”, in Little Dark Age, performed by MGMT:
      Don't take it the wrong way / I can never keep up / Sick of liking your selfies
    • 2022 July 3, Kalley Huang, “The Rise of the 0.5 Selfie”, in The New York Times‎[5], New York, N.Y.: The New York Times Company, →ISSN, →OCLC, archived from the original on 4 July 2025:
      Nothing is visible until the selfie is taken, which is half the fun. […] Posting the selfies on Instagram, where limbs are noodly or eyes are buggy, is meant to be silly, making it seem like the photographers take themselves — and social media — less seriously.

Usage notes

[edit]
  • Usage is very varied, including photos of oneself that are not taken by oneself (not self-portraits), as in “Could you take a selfie of me?” (compare autobiography, which may be written by a ghostwriter), or not only of oneself, as in “This is a selfie of me and my sister.” Many terms for recently popular photo genres have been coined by analogy by suffixing -ie, as in shelfie, or by blending, as in nelfie.[1] A self-portrait of multiple people is sometimes called an ussie, groupie, or selvesie.
